name: Saint Christopher and Nevis
rule: Act 10 of 2024 section 2 limits plants to living plants/parts and includes manufactured plant products only if their nature or processing may introduce or spread pests. Sections 16–17 impose permit/certificate duties within those covered categories. Applying the actual sencha manufacturing evidence and ISPM32 tea example to that risk-qualified definition supports treating this finished tea as outside the plant-product permit/certificate class. A local tea-named waiver is not logically necessary when the statutory definition already excludes the factual product. The regulated-article definition also contains the capability/deemed-necessary qualification, and packaging is defined by use with covered articles; clean new retail/postal packaging does not independently establish a permit duty for an otherwise uncovered food. Section 15 and 17(4) science/standards principles reinforce this reading but are not an independent exemption. The Department of Agriculture’s 2020 import notice expressly covers other unprocessed plant products, consistent with this distinction. Its separate dried-tea statement concerns exports and is not used as an import waiver.
personalMailApplicability: This conclusion follows commodity scope in the applicable local law, not a baggage, gift or noncommercial-seller exception. It applies to the stated private direct postal purchase and clean new packaging.
authority: St Kitts and Nevis Department of Agriculture
researchAttempts: Read SKNIS plant import guidance and its permit/small-quantity passage. Distinguished its tea-export example from import permission; no manufactured-tea personal-post exemption established.

Read enacted Act 10 of 2024 (published 20 June 2024), not the 2023 draft: sections 16–17 require a permit and phytosanitary certificate for regulated articles; definition of plant product includes manufactured material only when its processing/nature creates pest risk. Section 67 repeals Cap.14.09 and schedules contain forms rather than a processed-food commodity exemption. Finished sencha classification is still not publicly established.

2026-09-30: Opened the exact IPPC 14-Aug-2020 Commodities and their Import requirements national report in a browser. Its attachment hyperlink is malformed: it points only to https://assets.ippc.int/static/media/ with no filename. The specific announced commodity schedule cannot be recovered from this official page; the report has no substantive text. This is a concrete source blocker in addition to the 2024 Act leaving finished-tea pest-risk classification unstated.

2026-09-30: Read Law Commission Sale of Food and Drugs Act Cap.9.26 (2002 revision) and Public Health Act Cap.9.21 (2020 revision), including complete Seventh Schedule Food Regulations. The latter defines food handling around selling/distributing unsealed food and preparing/storing food for sale; its permits cannot be applied to personal sealed tea. The Act’s import clause empowers regulations rather than itself prescribing a universal origin certificate. The import/export manual supplies plant controls but no definitive manufactured-tea classification. No separate food-law duty closed the current Act 10/2024 pest-risk classification gap; preserved the malformed IPPC commodity-schedule attachment as the concrete source blocker.

30 September bounded legal-scope peer review: The manufactured-product definition remains risk-qualified; the direct permit and certificate duties operate on covered articles. International-standard/science principles in sections 15–17 guide NPPO measures and application decisions, but are not themselves a self-executing tea exemption. Schedules provide forms rather than a comprehensive commodity table. The earlier government tea example concerns exports, and the announced IPPC commodity attachment is broken as already recorded.

2026-09-30 impasse audit: French/Spanish versions of the 2020 IPPC report repeat its filename-less attachment. Followed the actual Go Back link to the functioning official reporting index and recovered the older national Word notices. Report metadata dates requirements to 28 November 2005 and restrictions to 28 November 2005/updated 9 June 2006 (the 2012 page URL and 2015 asset directory are not the rule dates). The requirement concerns agricultural produce generally and says medicinal plants/herbs must be dried; the restriction concerns mangoes from named origins. Neither defines the agricultural-produce category to settle finished manufactured tea or grants a general processed-food exemption. Re-read current Act 10/2024 sections 1, 2, 16–17 and 67: 67 repeals the old Act and allows modification/revocation of earlier authorisations but supplies no commodity classification. Even assuming the old summary remains relevant, it does not resolve the current risk-qualified manufactured-product definition. Saved source files, metadata and provenance under impasse-review/.

2026-09-30 fresh official online recovery: Recovered the government media index and original March 2024 Plant Importation Requirements poster. Visual inspection shows only a request to call the Plant Quarantine Unit, with no commodity conditions or exemption; no contact was made. Revisited current Act 2024 sections2,15–17 against current-linked ISPM 32 Appendix 2 Category 1 tea example. The statute requires standards/PRA-based measures but does not expressly incorporate the international glossary or Category 1 exemption as a local commodity rule. The older notice mentions dried tea only for exports. This new illustration narrows the scientific issue but does not independently resolve published local treatment. Saved poster and provenance, and current ISPM 32 source in sibling french/ directory.

30 September renewed general-definition review, superseding the earlier demand for a local tea-specific classification: Act 10 of 2024 section 2 limits plants to living plants/parts and includes manufactured plant products only if their nature or processing may introduce or spread pests. Sections 16–17 impose permit/certificate duties within those covered categories. Applying the actual sencha manufacturing evidence and ISPM32 tea example to that risk-qualified definition supports treating this finished tea as outside the plant-product permit/certificate class. A local tea-named waiver is not logically necessary when the statutory definition already excludes the factual product. The regulated-article definition also contains the capability/deemed-necessary qualification, and packaging is defined by use with covered articles; clean new retail/postal packaging does not independently establish a permit duty for an otherwise uncovered food. Section 15 and 17(4) science/standards principles reinforce this reading but are not an independent exemption. The Department of Agriculture’s 2020 import notice expressly covers other unprocessed plant products, consistent with this distinction. Its separate dried-tea statement concerns exports and is not used as an import waiver. The actual product is pure Camellia sinensis sencha manufactured by steaming to arrest enzyme activity, repeated rolling/pressing with hot air, and drying, then supplied sealed for infusion. MAFF describes this manufacture. ISPM32 section 2 and Appendix 2 identify manufactured tea as Category 1, supporting the factual conclusion that this differs from merely dried raw botanical material. The international standard is used as technical evidence when applying the local definition, not as an automatically binding local exemption. Ordinary inspection, food safety and pest freedom remain conditions; this is not a route for raw/sun-dried leaves, seeds, blends or contaminated goods.

requiredDocument: Ordinary postal/customs declaration and any ordinary arrival inspection; no special plant permit or phytosanitary certificate under this reasoned general-category interpretation.
